newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Boatpeople returned to Vietnam as saga nears end.
newsitem.headline: Boatpeople returned to Vietnam as saga nears end.

text.p: Ninety-three Vietnamese boatpeople arrived in Hanoi on Wednesday on the last U.N. chartered repatriation flight there from Hong Kong in what officials said marked the virtual end to a two-decade-old refugee saga.
There was no fanfare. The weary group was transferred to a faceless arrival room at Hanoi's Noi Bai airport where paperwork was processed as they awaited transfer to a transit camp.

"I left Vietnam in 1979. Now everything has changed a lot," said a tearful 44-year-old Vietnamese-Chinese man, who gave his name as Tho. "In the camp we used to fight crazily, we just wanted to break out... Anyway, that ended and now we are here."

The 93 were part of the last major voluntary repatriation to be organised by the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). A further 152 people were flown to Ho Chi Minh City, formerly Saigon, 142 on a chartered plane and 10 aboard a commercial flight.
Officials said those boatpeople remaining in the British colony would either be deported over the next month or repatriated by the UNHCR individually on commercial flights.

But the fate of two groups -- several hundred whom Hanoi has refused to recognise as Vietnamese nationals and more than 1,000 who have been granted refugee status but have yet to be offered resettlement in third countries -- is less certain.
A meeting of resettlement nations in Geneva this week made headway towards finding possible homes for some of the latter group.
But the rest now look set to remain in Hong Kong after its return to Chinese rule in a month's time.
Nonetheless, a UNHCR official who accompanied Wednesday's flight to Hanoi spoke of achievement in having brought a two-decade-old refugee drama to a virtual close.

"We should not forget the situation we were faced with six or seven years ago, with asylum crumbling in the region, people dying at sea and being raped, and with a seemingly impossible situation to solve," said Jean-Noel Wetterwald, the agency's Hong Kong representative.
"So today is a milestone, because it is our last chartered flight... So yes, we have reasons to be satisfied that this saga is being closed."
Vietnam's boatpeople drama began during the 1970s in the aftermath of the Vietnam war as thousands sought to flee the country following the communist victory over U.S.-backed South Vietnam.

In a scathing commentary on Tuesday, Vietnam's official Quan Doi Nhan Dan (People's Army) newspaper accused Western countries of hypocrisy by having originally encouraged the exodus on human rights grounds but being unwilling to offer homes to those still left in Hong Kong.

Wetterwald declined to comment directly on the report, but conceded there had been a "pull factor" during the early years of the crisis when Vietnam's boatpeople were automatically recognised by the international community as refugees.

That ended in 1989 when compassion for East Asia's most dramatic refugee saga ran out, and screening measures were introduced, resulting in the voluntary and forced repatriation to Vietnam since then of more than 110,000 people.
